scope: Annotated bibliography and narrative calibration for external finance to India: the academic and memoir literature on IMF/World Bank conditionality (Kentikelenis & Stubbs; Kapur, Lewis & Webb; Kirk; Bhagwati & Panagariya; Ahluwalia; Rangarajan; Y.V. Reddy), on Chinese official finance (Dreher et al.; AidData GCDF 3.0; Brookings 2020) and on procurement red flags (Fazekas & Kocsis); the primary records that calibrate six circulating narratives (OED/IEG India Country Assistance Evaluation 2001; the World Bank GIA verification of Doing Business irregularities 2020-12-08; the Supreme Court's interim order in State of Kerala v Union of India 2024-04-01; the Resilient Kerala DPO program document 2019; JICA MAHSR tranche V 2023; AIIB 2020 loans); and the open datasets with their licences. It records works as `mechanism` nodes and only office-holders as persons. It leaves out: project-level lending (worldbank.json, worldbank-projects.json, adb-aiib.json, bilateral-china.json), contract awards (contracts.json), and IMF primary documents (imf.org blocked from this environment). Web search was capped for the session, so the sweep used known URLs; the CAG audit of externally aided projects, the IEG country evaluations after 2001, the Indian long-reads on the bullet-train loan and AIIB, and the Kapur–Webb G-24 paper could not be opened and are recorded as gaps.

entities.label: IMF
entities.sub: International Monetary Fund — balance-of-payments lender; conditionality
entities.publicRole: Multilateral lender whose 1981 EFF and 1991 stand-by arrangement with India are the canonical Indian cases of policy conditionality; imf.org is blocked from this environment so its record here comes from the IMF Monitor dataset, memoirs and encyclopaedic summaries
d: Attached 65,894 policy conditions to its lending programmes between 1980 and 2019 according to the IMF Monitor dataset (Kentikelenis & Stubbs) [reported]
Lent India an emergency package in 1991 against which the RBI pledged 67 tonnes of gold; Wikipedia gives the loan as US$7 billion — unverified against IMF documents [reported]
Ahluwalia was the first director of its Independent Evaluation Office (2001–2004-06) and 'supervised several studies critical of various aspects of the functioning of the IMF' [reported]

Its Development Policy Financing disburses 'non-earmarked general budget financing' against prior actions and 'maintenance of an adequate macroeconomic policy framework, as determined by the Bank with inputs from IMF assessments' [documented]

Management reconfirmed that they were not data irregularities during GIA's verification' [documented]

entities.label: OED — India: Country Assistance Evaluation (Report No. 22134, 2001-04-23)
entities.sub: The World Bank's own evaluation of its India programme in the 1990s
entities.publicRole: The lender's ex-post verdict on conditionality, state selection and procurement in India — the primary text behind three of the six narratives
d: Outcome 'moderately satisfactory for the decade as a whole'; efficacy 'modest, mainly on account of the Bank's limited impact on fiscal and other structural reforms' [documented]

'Conditionality was used sparingly and the commonality between the Bank's objectives and the government's was continually stressed'; Bank anti-poverty ambitions 'were, however, resisted by the authorities, who feared Bank interference in politically sensitive national programs' [documented]

1997 CAS pillar: 'concentration of assistance toward states and programs strongly committed to reform' → comprehensive reform programmes in Andhra Pradesh, Uttar Pradesh and Karnataka, close engagement with Orissa and Rajasthan [documented]
FY98 commitments of US$2.1 billion 'much lower than planned' because of sanctions by major shareholders after the May 1998 nuclear tests; only 'basic human needs' projects allowed [documented]

'Only 56% of the 50 evaluated projects in FY96-00 obtained satisfactory Bank performance at appraisal ratings compared to 61% in FY90-94'; 'implementation problems, chiefly among them procurement delays' — 'weaknesses in preparing bid documents and in contracting procedures, and delays in contract awards following bid evaluation' [documented]

claims.lab: 1991 IMF emergency financing (stand-by arrangement and related facilities)

narratives.claim: Multilateral loans come with policy strings that override Parliament.
narratives.strongestCase: Conditionality is real and documented: the IMF Monitor dataset codes 65,894 conditions in IMF programmes 1980–2019; the 1991 IMF/World Bank package was followed within weeks by the 1991-07-24 Budget's deregulation, 51% foreign-equity and disinvestment measures; World Bank DPF still disburses only on 'completion of a set of critical policy and institutional actions agreed between the Bank and the client' and 'maintenance of an adequate macroeconomic policy framework, as determined by the Bank with inputs from IMF assessments'. The Kerala DPO's eight prior actions are state policy acts. Loan agreements are signed by the executive under Article 292/293 with no parliamentary ratification, and Parliament has never legislated the borrowing limit Article 292 permits.
narratives.strongestCounter: 'Override' is the wrong verb. The Bank's own evaluator found that in India 'Conditionality was used sparingly and the commonality between the Bank's objectives and the government's was continually stressed', and that Bank ambitions were 'resisted by the authorities'. DPF is 'non-earmarked general budget financing that is subject to the borrower's own implementation processes' with a stated 'country ownership' principle; prior actions are drafted from the borrower's programme (Kerala's RKDP). The 1991 reforms were argued for by Indian economists before the crisis (Bhagwati–Panagariya; Ahluwalia; Rangarajan) and legislated where legislation was needed. The clearest external constraint on Bank lending to India — the 1998 nuclear-test sanctions — came from shareholder politics, not loan covenants. Parliament is bypassed by India's own executive treaty-making design, not by lenders.
narratives.whatWouldChangeThis: Up to well-supported: an Indian statute or budget provision documented as enacted to satisfy a specific prior action against the recorded position of the ministry or a parliamentary committee (e.g. a DPL matrix line matched to a bill's statement of objects). Down to unsupported: the IMF Monitor India rows showing condition counts at or below programme means and no structural conditions in 1991 beyond the government's own Letter of Intent.

narratives.claim: Lender-funded contracts go to a closed club of contractors.
narratives.strongestCase: For tied bilateral loans it is true by construction: JICA's MAHSR tranches state 'Procurement: Tied', restricting suppliers to Japanese firms in exchange for 0.1%/50-year money. For multilateral loans, Fazekas & Kocsis show that single bidding, short advertisement periods and procedure choice are measurable red flags of 'unjustified restriction of access to public contracts', and contracts.json records recurring winners and World Bank debarments of Indian firms. The OED found India's bid documents and contracting procedures weak in the 1990s.
narratives.strongestCounter: The lender's own diagnosis of Indian procurement failure is delay — 'weaknesses in preparing bid documents ... and delays in contract awards following bid evaluation' — not capture. Multilateral procurement is open to all member-country bidders with published awards and a sanctions system, which is more transparent than most domestic procurement; a recurring set of large winners (L&T, Afcons, Tata Projects) is what a thin market for complex civil works looks like anywhere. Fazekas & Kocsis is a European study; no India single-bidding rate for lender-funded contracts has been computed in this fleet yet.
narratives.whatWouldChangeThis: Up to well-supported: World Bank/ADB contract-award data for India showing single-bid or repeat-winner rates materially above the Bank-wide or CPPP baseline in the same sectors. Down to unsupported: rates at or below baseline, with the recurring winners explained by prequalification thresholds.

narratives.claim: External borrowing under the NDA is more concessional / less than under the UPA.
narratives.strongestCase: Under NDA India signed the most concessional large loan in its history (JICA MAHSR: 0.1%, 50 years, 15-year grace) and used IDA blend terms by exception (Kerala 2019); the AIIB and NDB were added as lenders; DPOs brought budget support at IBRD rates.
narratives.strongestCounter: The direction is mixed and the driver is structural: India graduated to 'only IBRD financial terms' on income grounds, so the concessional share of multilateral borrowing fell across the 2014 boundary regardless of government; JICA yen loans are concessional but tied; AIIB/NDB lend at near-IBRD terms. No consolidated series (DEA External Debt Status Report concessional-debt share, 2004–2026) was opened in this sweep, so neither 'more' nor 'less' has a denominator here.
narratives.whatWouldChangeThis: The RBI/DEA external-debt releases for end-March 2004, 2014 and 2025 (concessional share, multilateral vs bilateral, average terms of new commitments) plus the worldbank-projects.json instrument mix by year would settle the volume and terms comparison; a discontinuity at 2014 not explained by IDA graduation would move it to contested; a smooth trend would move it to debunked as a partisan claim.

narratives.claim: Opposition-run states are denied external loans by the Centre (the DEA approval bottleneck).
narratives.strongestCase: The mechanism exists and bites: all state borrowing including externally aided projects needs Union consent under Article 293(3); the DEA fixed Kerala's FY2023-24 ceiling at ₹32,442 crore and counted off-budget (KIIFB-type) borrowings within it; Kerala sued, claiming ₹24,434 crore of denied space and 'extreme financial hardship'; the Supreme Court found the constitutional question serious enough for a five-judge bench. The World Bank's own 1990s practice of concentrating on 'reforming states' shows that state selection has always been discretionary.
narratives.strongestCounter: No lender document, DEA file or minister's statement records a partisan ground for refusing a state's project; the same Union routed a US$250m IDA-blend DPO to LDF-run Kerala in 2019; the ceiling is a 3%-of-GSDP FRBM/Finance Commission rule applying to every state; the Court found prima facie merit in the Union's case that Kerala had over-borrowed in FY2017-18 to FY2019-20 and had 'no unutilized fiscal space'; and the Bank's 1990s focus states were governed by parties across the spectrum. The 'denial' Kerala documents is of borrowing room, not of external projects.
narratives.whatWouldChangeThis: Up to contested/well-supported: a state-wise table of DEA-posed and approved EAPs 2014–2026 against population and prior lending showing a gap for opposition-run states that persists after controlling for fiscal indicators, or the Constitution Bench holding the ceiling's off-budget inclusion unconstitutional. Down to unsupported: the same table showing no gap.

narratives.claim: Chinese money captured Indian infrastructure companies before 2020.
narratives.strongestCase: Brookings (2020): official Chinese FDI rose five-fold to US$8bn by 2017 and 'at least US$26 billion' counting announcements; infrastructure investment was 'dominated by state-owned enterprises'; Chinese state banks were major creditors of private Indian power and telecom groups (Reliance Power/Sasan, RCom, Lanco, Adani Power Maharashtra — bilateral-china.json), and a UK court ordered Anil Ambani to pay US$717m to Chinese banks in 2020; Banking on Beijing documents the risks of 'political capture' in China's debt-financed model; Press Note 3 (2020) was the government's own response.
narratives.strongestCounter: 'Captured' means control, and no documented case shows a Chinese state entity taking control of a listed Indian infrastructure operator: the money was Other Official Flows — commercial equipment-linked credit to private borrowers, priced as such — and the realised FDI was mostly consumer-technology and pharma equity; the largest 'infrastructure' numbers are pledged and unapproved (≈US$15bn). Creditor power over a defaulting borrower (the Ambani judgment) is what any lender has. Brookings itself recommends openness with safeguards, not a capture finding.
narratives.whatWouldChangeThis: Up to contested: a documented change of control, board seat or step-in right exercised by a Chinese state lender over an Indian infrastructure company before 2020 (RoC filings, exchange disclosures). Down to debunked: AidData GCDF 3.0 India rows and DPIIT data confirming that pre-2020 Chinese official finance to Indian infrastructure was credit without equity or control rights.

narratives.claim: The World Bank's Doing Business ranking was gamed for India.
narratives.strongestCase: India's rank rose from 142 (DB2015) to 63 (DB2020) across exactly the editions (DB2018, DB2020) later found to contain manipulated data; the government used the rank as a performance claim; the WilmerHale report (per Wikipedia) found senior Bank leadership had pressured staff to change China's data, proving the index could be bent for a large borrower; India (Mumbai) does appear in the GIA report's list of DB16 data changes and a DB17 India construction-permits methodology concern was raised by the DB team itself.
narratives.strongestCounter: The primary audit record names exactly four countries — Azerbaijan, Saudi Arabia and UAE (DB2020) and China (DB2018–20) — for nine irregularities, and India is not among them: the DB16 India (Mumbai) Getting Electricity item was one of five routine data changes reviewed, and management 'reconfirmed' the DB17 construction-permits concern 'were not data irregularities during GIA's verification'. Neither the 2021-09-16 discontinuation statement nor the Wikipedia summary of WilmerHale mentions India. India's rise coincided with documented reforms (insolvency code, GST, Delhi/Mumbai permit and electricity reforms) that the methodology rewarded.
narratives.whatWouldChangeThis: Up to contested: the WilmerHale report or the DEC review showing that the DB16 India (Mumbai) change or the DB17 construction-permits treatment favoured India against the methodology, or evidence of Indian government pressure on Bank leadership comparable to the China finding. Down to debunked: release of the full DEC review confirming India's items were methodology-compliant.

symmetryCheck: UPA vs NDA: the strongest documented case of external policy conditions shaping Indian law is the 1991 IMF/World Bank package under a Congress government (Rao/Singh), and the World Bank's own evaluator says even then 'Conditionality was used sparingly'; the NDA-era DPOs (Kerala 2019, PMGKY and MSME 2020, low-carbon 2023 — worldbank.json) carry prior actions drawn from the government's own programmes. The 'strings' lens applied to the UPA control produces the more alarming picture, which is a finding about the lens: it detects crisis-year borrowing, not party. BJP-run vs opposition-run states: the one litigated case of Union restriction (Kerala, 2023–24) sits beside a 2019 IDA-blend DPO to the same opposition-run state, and the Bank's 1990s focus states spanned TDP, BJP, BSP, Janata Dal, Congress and BJD governments; no partisan pattern is documented, and the analytic gap remains open until the state-wise EAP table is built. Chinese vs Japanese money: the 'closed club' and 'capture' lenses run on the Japanese control produce a literal contractual closed club (tied MAHSR procurement) and a 50-year creditor relationship with a Union PSU — more concentrated than anything documented for Chinese credit to Indian private firms — so the alarm the lens raises for China is a property of the lens unless control rights are shown. Doing Business: the countries the audit names are China, Azerbaijan, Saudi Arabia and the UAE; India is reviewed and cleared.
